episode_title: 446. Single Seat, No Second Chances: Air Vice Marshal Sean Bell

real_qa.q: How do you lead pilots when flying the Harrier jet loses three aircraft per year due to aircrew error, while maintaining their confidence to fly?
real_qa.r: The reality was there was no leadership challenge because people were willingly doing it and egging each other on. During the Cold War, pilots felt they were the tip of the sword and needed to be ready for Soviet invasion at any moment, so they pushed very hard despite the risks. The irony was that although statistics showed many would be killed, everybody went out willingly because they understood the existential threat and believed in their mission.
real_qa.requete: Harrier jet aircrew error leadership confidence

real_qa.q: What specific cultural practices did Joint Force Harrier use to integrate RAF and Royal Navy pilots beyond spreadsheet reorganization?
real_qa.r: Joint Force Harrier held Trafalgar Night in the mess with naval traditions like models of aircraft and flower bomb celebrations, which was foreign to RAF culture but created pride. They also put together a Joint Force team in the field gun races at Portsmouth, and the commander would present shirts to competitors, creating symbols of unity. These traditions had nothing to do with work operations but were everything for encouraging that spirit of togetherness and unity of purpose across the two tribes.
real_qa.requete: Joint Force Harrier RAF Royal Navy integration culture

real_qa.q: When did Air Vice Marshal Sean Bell transition from flying Harrier jets to commanding as a station commander, and why did he reduce his flying hours?
real_qa.r: The major transition happened when Bell became station commander, a flying appointment where he was still expected to fly but ended up flying less than he could have. His conscious decision was that if he flew more hours, fewer would be available for junior pilots, and in wartime, the younger pilots should go while he provided support from behind. He believed his job was to be the grown-up behind the scenes rather than sit in the jet at the front, despite criticism from his two-star boss.
real_qa.requete: station commander Harrier flying hours transition

real_qa.q: What did Air Vice Marshal Sean Bell learn about managing risk appetite in military operations versus peacetime wars of choice?
real_qa.r: Bell observed that because modern conflicts are wars of choice rather than wars of national survival, risk appetite has dropped significantly in the military. The benefit is fewer accidents, but the downside is less preparation for existential threats. He notes that the longer people are out on operations, the more their risk appetite gradually drifts up, and there's a need for regular revisiting of risk processes and ensuring commander's intent remains omnipresent, felt, articulated, and owned rather than just captured in documents.
real_qa.requete: military risk appetite wars of choice national survival

real_qa.q: Why did Air Vice Marshal Sean Bell refuse to rename RAF Cottesmore as a Royal Navy facility when integrating Joint Force Harrier?
real_qa.r: Bell looked incredulous when the Royal Navy requested changing the base name from Royal Air Force Cottesmore because there were 2,000 people on the base and the Navy was only a small part of it. Although Bell won the battle as the senior commander, he reflected afterwards that he did not really win because the decision caused a bigger point for people. He learned more from this failure than from successes, recognizing that harsh treatment of mistakes creates a culture where people avoid taking risks.
real_qa.requete: RAF Cottesmore Joint Force Harrier base naming dispute

guest.bio_context: Sean Bell commanded Number 1 Fighter Squadron, the oldest in the Royal Air Force, and then Joint Force Harrier, bringing RAF and Royal Navy together under one command. He flew the Harrier single-seat jet and completed three tours of Afghanistan, as well as operations in Bosnia, Kosovo, and Iraq. He finished his military career as an Air Vice Marshal and is now founder of Loyal Wingman, a charity saving the lives of Ukrainian aircrew. He is a regular analyst on Sky News and the BBC explaining global conflicts.

real_quote: I remember I learned more from my failures than I ever learned from my successes, and I joined an environment of service which tended to be very harsh on people who made mistakes.
